questions.stem: To be counted as employed in the ABS Labour Force Survey, a person aged 15 or over must have, in the reference week:
options: worked at least 15 hours for pay
worked for at least one hour for pay
worked at least 35 hours for pay
held a permanent job for at least a month
questions.explanation: The ABS counts anyone aged 15 or over who worked at least one hour for pay, profit or payment in kind in the reference week as employed. Thirty-five hours is the usual dividing line between full-time and part-time work, not the test for being employed.

questions.stem: The ABS counts a person as unemployed if they are not employed and they:
options: are under 65 and have not worked in the past year
have actively looked for work and are available to start
are receiving an unemployment payment from the government
would like a job but have stopped looking for one
questions.explanation: To be unemployed, a person must be without work, actively looking for it and available to start. Someone who wants a job but has given up looking is not in the labour force, so they are not counted as unemployed.

questions.stem: A town has a working-age population of 20,000, of whom 12,000 are employed and 800 are unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
questions.explanation: The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed, 12,800, and the unemployment rate is 800 ÷ 12,800 × 100 = 6.25%. Dividing by the working-age population gives 4%, but people outside the labour force are not counted in the rate.

questions.stem: In a region, the working-age population is 50,000 and the labour force is 32,000. The participation rate is:
questions.explanation: The participation rate is the labour force as a percentage of the working-age population: 32,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 64%. The 36% is the share not in the labour force.

questions.stem: Jess works 12 hours a week in retail but wants, and is available for, 30 hours. The ABS classes her as:
options: employed and fully utilised
not in the labour force
employed and underemployed
unemployed, as she works part-time
questions.explanation: Jess has worked at least one hour, so she is employed, but she wants and is available for more hours, so she is underemployed. Part-time workers are employed, not unemployed, which is why underemployment is measured separately.

questions.stem: A car manufacturing plant closes as production moves overseas, and its workers lack the skills that growing industries need. Their unemployment is best described as:
options: structural
cyclical
frictional
seasonal
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs available after the economy's structure changes. Cyclical unemployment is caused by a downturn in overall demand, which would ease when the economy recovers.

questions.stem: Which change in the labour market is driven mainly by technology?
options: an increase in the minimum wage decided in the annual wage review
automation replacing routine tasks while creating demand for digital skills
a seasonal rise in fruit-picking jobs in regional areas during each harvest
a fall in the share of people of working age as the population ages
questions.explanation: Automation and digital technology change which tasks need people and which skills employers seek. Population ageing also changes the labour market, but its cause is demographic, not technological.

questions.stem: The growth of the 'gig economy' refers to:
options: more businesses moving their production from Australia to factories overseas
more people doing short-term tasks, often through apps, without ongoing employment
more people working in permanent full-time jobs with paid annual and sick leave
more workers joining trade unions so that they can bargain together for wages
questions.explanation: Gig work, such as rideshare driving and food delivery, is paid task by task, often through digital platforms, usually without the leave and security of ongoing employment. It is part of the shift towards more flexible and less secure work.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects a business perspective on a rise in the minimum wage?
options: higher pay will reduce the government's spending on welfare payments
higher wages will lower costs of production for most Australian firms
higher wage costs may squeeze profits and lead some firms to cut hours
higher pay will make it easier for low-paid workers to meet living costs
questions.explanation: For employers, a higher minimum wage raises labour costs, which may reduce profits or lead them to cut hours, hiring or both. Meeting living costs is the perspective of workers and households, not of businesses.

questions.stem: Which government response is mainly aimed at reducing structural unemployment?
options: raising unemployment payments so that jobseekers can meet their costs
lowering income tax rates to raise households' disposable income
funding retraining in the skills that growing industries need
increasing government spending during a recession to boost demand
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch of skills, so retraining tackles its cause directly. Extra spending and tax cuts during a downturn target cyclical unemployment, which stems from weak demand.

questions.stem: Why is high unemployment a concern for the national economy, not only for those without work?
options: it raises productivity across the economy, as fewer workers share the capital
lost output lowers living standards, and welfare costs rise as tax revenue falls
unemployed workers raise inflation by spending more than employed workers do
it shrinks the labour force, which then lowers the unemployment rate further
questions.explanation: Idle workers mean goods and services that could have been produced are lost, while the government pays more in benefits and collects less tax. Unemployed people have lower incomes and spend less, so high unemployment tends to lower inflation rather than raise it.

questions.stem: A country has a comparative advantage in producing a good when it:
options: has larger reserves of natural resources than any other country
can sell it on world markets at a higher price than other countries
can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than other countries
can produce more of it than any other country with the same resources
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost: a country should specialise in what it gives up least to produce. Producing more with the same resources is absolute advantage, which is not needed for gains from trade.

questions.stem: With the same resources, Australia can produce 10 tonnes of wheat or 5 cars, and Japan 6 tonnes of wheat or 6 cars. Which statement is correct?
options: Australia should specialise in cars and Japan in wheat
Australia should produce both, as it has an absolute advantage in both
Neither country gains from trade, as Japan produces cars more efficiently
Australia should specialise in wheat and Japan in cars
questions.explanation: In Australia a tonne of wheat costs 0.5 cars, while in Japan it costs 1 car, so Australia has the comparative advantage in wheat and Japan in cars. Australia has an absolute advantage only in wheat, because Japan makes more cars with the same resources.

questions.stem: International trade based on specialisation is expected to raise living standards mainly because:
options: trade guarantees that every worker in each country keeps their existing job
total output rises when each country produces what it makes at the lowest opportunity cost
each country becomes self-sufficient and produces all the goods it consumes
every country is able to sell its exports for more than it pays for its imports
questions.explanation: Specialising according to comparative advantage lets the world produce more from the same resources, and trade lets each country consume beyond its own production possibilities. Trade also shifts resources between industries, so some workers lose jobs even as overall living standards rise.

questions.stem: A tariff is:
options: a tax on goods that are exported overseas
a tax on imported goods
a limit on the quantity of goods imported
a payment to local producers to cut their costs
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports, raising their price in the local market and protecting local producers. A limit on the quantity imported is a quota.

questions.stem: The government places a tariff on imported steel. The most likely effects are:
options: higher steel prices for local buyers and more sales for local producers
lower steel prices for local buyers and fewer sales for local producers
higher steel prices for local buyers and fewer sales for local producers
lower prices for imported steel and higher tax revenue for exporters
questions.explanation: The tariff raises the price of imported steel, so local producers can sell more, often at higher prices, while local buyers of steel pay more. The tax revenue goes to the government, not to exporters.

questions.stem: An import quota protects local producers by:
options: taxing each unit of a good that is brought into the country
paying local producers a set amount for each unit produced
requiring imported goods to meet stricter safety standards
limiting the quantity of a good that can be imported
questions.explanation: A quota sets a maximum quantity of imports, so local producers face less competition. Taxing each imported unit is a tariff, and paying local producers per unit is a subsidy.

questions.stem: A free trade agreement between Australia and another country mainly:
options: reduces or removes tariffs and other barriers to trade between them
requires the two countries to adopt the same currency as each other
fixes the exchange rate between the two countries' currencies
requires each country to buy a set value of the other's exports
questions.explanation: Free trade agreements lower tariffs, quotas and other barriers so goods, services and investment flow more easily between the countries. They do not create a shared currency or fix exchange rates, which are separate arrangements.

questions.stem: A proposal to remove the tariff on imported clothing is most likely to be opposed by:
options: overseas firms that export clothing to Australia
local clothing manufacturers and their workers
households that buy clothing for their families
retailers that import clothing to sell in stores
questions.explanation: Removing the tariff exposes local manufacturers to cheaper imports, threatening their sales and their workers' jobs. Households, importing retailers and overseas exporters all gain from cheaper imported clothing.

questions.stem: A fall in the value of the Australian dollar is most likely to benefit:
options: Australian exporters, as their goods become cheaper for overseas buyers
Australian importers, as overseas goods become cheaper for them to buy
Australian tourists, as travel overseas becomes cheaper for them
Australian firms that rely heavily on imported parts and materials
questions.explanation: A lower dollar means foreign buyers need less of their own currency to buy Australian goods, so exports become more competitive. Imports, overseas travel and imported inputs all become dearer, not cheaper.

questions.stem: Why might a regional town that depends on one export industry be especially affected by changes in international trade?
options: a fall in world demand or prices for that export can cut local jobs and incomes
exports produced in regional areas are not counted as part of Australia's GDP
regional towns must pay higher tariffs on their exports than capital cities do
a rise in world prices for that export always lowers incomes in the local area
questions.explanation: When a town's jobs and incomes depend on one export, falling world demand or prices flow quickly through to local employment and spending. This local exposure is one reason trade is important at local, national and international levels. Higher world prices would tend to raise local incomes, not lower them.

questions.stem: A government protects a new local electric vehicle industry with tariffs until it can compete with established overseas producers. This uses the:
options: comparative advantage argument
infant industry argument
national security argument
anti-dumping argument
questions.explanation: The infant industry argument holds that a new industry needs temporary protection until it grows large and efficient enough to compete. The anti-dumping argument applies when overseas firms sell below cost, which is not the case here.

questions.stem: The difference between income and wealth is that:
options: income includes only wages and salaries, while wealth includes only property
income is measured before tax is paid, while wealth is measured after tax
income is a flow received over time, while wealth is a stock of assets at a point in time
income is held in the form of assets, while wealth is received over a period of time
questions.explanation: Income, such as wages, rent and dividends, is received over a period, while wealth is the value of assets minus liabilities at a point in time. Wealth includes shares, superannuation and savings as well as property.

questions.stem: A Gini coefficient of 0 indicates:
options: perfect equality, with income shared equally by everyone
perfect inequality, with one person holding all the income
that no income at all was earned in the economy that year
that average income grew by zero per cent over the year
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient runs from 0, perfect equality, to 1, where one person receives all income. A higher coefficient means a more unequal distribution.

questions.stem: A country's Gini coefficient for income rises from 0.32 to 0.36. This shows that:
options: the poorest households have lost income
income has become less equally distributed
income has become more equally distributed
average income has risen by about 4 per cent
questions.explanation: A higher Gini coefficient means income is shared less equally. The coefficient measures the spread of income, not its level, so it says nothing directly about average income or whether the poorest households lost income.

questions.stem: On a Lorenz curve diagram, the further the Lorenz curve lies from the line of equality, the:
options: higher the average income per person
lower the value of the Gini coefficient
more unequal the distribution of income
more equal the distribution of income
questions.explanation: The line of equality shows every group receiving an equal share, so a Lorenz curve that bows further away shows greater inequality. A larger gap between the curve and the line means a higher Gini coefficient, not a lower one.

questions.stem: In a country, the top 20% of households receive 40% of income and the bottom 20% receive 8%. How many times larger is the top quintile's share than the bottom quintile's?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so the top fifth receives five times the share of the bottom fifth. Thirty-two is the gap in percentage points, not the ratio, and 0.2 is the ratio inverted.

questions.stem: Which is an example of income from the ownership of capital or property?
options: the value of a family home that is owned outright
dividends from shares and rent from an investment property
wages and salaries earned in return for working in a job
the age pension and other government transfer payments
questions.explanation: Dividends and rent are returns on owning assets. The value of a home is part of wealth, a stock, rather than income, which is a flow received over time.

questions.stem: Which factor is most likely to widen wealth inequality over time?
options: faster wage growth for the lowest-paid workers than for the highest-paid workers
rising house and share prices, which mostly benefit those who already own assets
a more progressive income tax system that taxes high incomes at higher rates
higher means-tested payments to low-income families with dependent children
questions.explanation: Asset price growth adds most to the wealth of those who already own homes and shares, so the gap with non-owners widens. A more progressive tax, means-tested payments and faster wage growth for the lowest-paid all tend to narrow inequality.

questions.stem: A progressive income tax is one in which:
options: everyone pays the same dollar amount of tax each year
higher incomes pay a higher percentage of income in tax
everyone pays the same percentage of their income in tax
lower incomes pay a higher percentage of income in tax
questions.explanation: Under a progressive tax, the average tax rate rises as income rises, which redistributes income and narrows inequality. A tax taking the same percentage from everyone is proportional, and one taking a larger share from lower incomes is regressive.

questions.stem: The GST is often described as regressive because:
options: the rate of GST falls as the income of the household paying it rises
lower-income households spend more of their income, so pay more GST relative to income
higher-income households pay a higher GST rate when they buy luxury goods
the GST is charged only on goods that low-income households tend to buy
questions.explanation: The GST has one rate, but lower-income households spend a larger share of their income, so GST takes a larger percentage of their income. The rate does not change with income or with the type of good bought.

questions.stem: An economist supports transfer payments targeted at need rather than identical payments to everyone. She is prioritising:
options: growth, meaning a higher level of real GDP over time
equity, meaning fairness, rather than strict equality
equality, meaning that everyone receives exactly the same
efficiency, meaning maximum output from scarce resources
questions.explanation: Equity is about fairness, which can mean giving more to those with greater need, while equality means identical shares. Targeting by need is a judgement about fairness, not about maximising output.

questions.stem: Critics of very high top marginal tax rates argue that they may lower living standards because they:
options: make the income tax system much less progressive than it was before
can weaken incentives to work, invest and take risks, reducing output
increase the amount that high-income earners spend on goods and services
raise the incomes of high earners compared with those of low earners
questions.explanation: If people keep less of each extra dollar, some may work, invest or start businesses less, reducing output; this is the trade-off between equity and efficiency. Higher top rates make the tax system more progressive, not less.

questions.stem: Sustainable development is best defined as development that:
options: occurs only in countries that generate all of their energy from renewables
meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
maximises the rate of economic growth over the shortest possible period of time
stops all use of non-renewable resources immediately, whatever the cost
questions.explanation: Sustainable development balances meeting today's needs with protecting the resources and environment future generations depend on. It does not require growth to stop, or all non-renewable resource use to end at once.

questions.stem: Which is a non-renewable resource?
options: solar energy
wind energy
plantation timber
natural gas
questions.explanation: Natural gas formed over millions of years and is used far faster than it forms, so it is non-renewable. Sun and wind are not used up, and plantation timber can be regrown.

questions.stem: A factory's emissions harm the health of nearby residents, who are not part of the factory's transactions. This is an example of:
options: a positive externality
a public good
price discrimination
a negative externality
questions.explanation: A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties who are not part of a transaction and receive no compensation. A positive externality would be a benefit to third parties, such as the wider gains from vaccination.

questions.stem: When producing a good creates pollution that the producer does not pay for, a free market tends to:
options: overproduce the good, as its price does not reflect the full cost to society
underproduce the good, as its price reflects a cost that is far too high
produce the efficient quantity, as consumers are choosing freely
stop producing the good altogether, as pollution raises its price
questions.explanation: Because the producer ignores the cost of pollution, the market price is too low and too much is produced, a form of market failure. The good would be underproduced only if its price overstated its true cost.

questions.stem: Fish stocks in an unregulated area of ocean collapse as each fishing fleet catches as much as it can before others do. This illustrates:
options: the tragedy of the commons
the law of diminishing returns
the infant industry argument
the endowment effect
questions.explanation: When a shared resource is open to all, each user gains from taking more while the cost of depletion is spread across everyone, so the resource is overused. Clear rules or property rights, such as fishing quotas, are common responses.

questions.stem: A carbon tax is designed to reduce emissions mainly by:
options: setting a fixed number of permits that firms trade with each other
raising the cost of emitting, so firms and households emit less
banning firms from emitting more than a set limit each year
paying firms a subsidy for each tonne of carbon they emit
questions.explanation: A carbon tax puts a price on each tonne emitted, giving firms and households an incentive to cut emissions wherever that is cheaper than paying. Tradeable permits under a cap are the mechanism of an emissions trading scheme, not a tax.

questions.stem: Under a cap-and-trade emissions trading scheme, a firm that can cut its emissions cheaply is most likely to:
options: be exempted from the cap altogether because its abatement costs are low
reduce its emissions and sell spare permits to firms facing higher costs
buy extra permits from other firms so that it can increase its emissions
pay a fixed tax on each tonne it emits, at a rate set by the government
questions.explanation: If cutting emissions costs the firm less than the market price of a permit, it profits by cutting and selling its unused permits. Emissions are therefore cut where it is cheapest to do so, while the cap fixes the total.

questions.stem: The key difference between a carbon tax and an emissions trading scheme is that:
options: a tax raises no revenue, while a trading scheme always raises revenue
a tax fixes the price of emissions, while a trading scheme fixes the quantity
a tax fixes the quantity of emissions, while a trading scheme fixes the price
a tax applies only to households, while a trading scheme applies to farms
questions.explanation: A carbon tax sets the price per tonne and lets the quantity of emissions adjust, while a cap-and-trade scheme sets the total quantity and lets the permit price adjust. A tax raises revenue on every tonne emitted.

questions.stem: Government subsidies for household rooftop solar panels aim to:
options: raise their price, reducing household use of grid power
tax households that use coal-fired electricity heavily
limit the number of panels each household can install
lower their cost to households, increasing their uptake
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers the effective price of solar panels, so more households find them worth installing, which reduces emissions from grid electricity. Subsidies work by lowering prices, not raising them.

questions.stem: Which group is most likely to oppose a high price on carbon emissions?
options: the operators of hydro-electric power stations
owners and workers of coal-fired power stations
manufacturers of wind turbines and solar panels
investors in new renewable energy projects
questions.explanation: A carbon price raises costs most for the highest emitters, threatening the profits and jobs of coal-fired generation. Renewable producers, including hydro-electric generators, gain because their low-emission electricity becomes more competitive.

questions.stem: Why is international cooperation, such as the Paris Agreement, seen as important in reducing greenhouse gas emissions?
options: only the countries that sign international agreements experience climate change
international agreements set a single world price for every good that is traded
emissions from each country remain within that country's own national borders
emissions affect the whole planet, so one country's cuts can be undone by others' increases
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases mix in the global atmosphere, so climate change is a global externality that no country can solve alone. Without cooperation, each country has an incentive to let others bear the cost of cutting emissions.
